subject: Weekly Revision
summary: all five topics of Week 7: first law for closed systems and control volumes; second law and entropy; differential equations; availability and thermodynamic relations; 1-D steady conduction (3 questions each)

questions.text: A rigid, insulated tank holds 0.8 kg of air (c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K). A paddle wheel driven from outside, as shown, does 40 kJ of work on the air. The rise in air temperature (in K, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: First law, closed system: Q − W = ΔU. Rigid tank → no boundary work, but shaft (paddle) work is still work.
Q = 0, W = −40 kJ (work done on the air), so ΔU = +40 kJ
Exam tip: 'Rigid' kills only p dV work; paddle-wheel and electrical work still cross the boundary.

questions.text: A closed system goes from state 1 to state 2 along different paths. Which quantity is the same for every path?
solution: Concept: Q and W are path functions (inexact differentials), but their difference equals ΔU.
Since U is a property, Q − W = U₂ − U₁ is fixed by the end states alone.
Exam tip: This is the first law's corollary: energy (U) is a property of the system.

questions.text: Air enters an adiabatic diffuser at 250 m/s and leaves at 30 m/s (c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K). The rise in air temperature (in K, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: SFEE with Q = W = 0 and Δz = 0: h₁ + V₁²/2 = h₂ + V₂²/2.
Exam tip: Use cp in J/kg·K (1005) when velocities are in m/s.

questions.text: For an adiabatic process in a closed system, the entropy of the system
opts: may decrease if the process is irreversible
remains constant if reversible and increases if irreversible
questions.ans: (C) remains constant if reversible and increases if irreversible
solution: Concept: ΔS = ∫δQ/T + Sgen. With δQ = 0, ΔS = Sgen ≥ 0.
Reversible adiabatic (isentropic): S<sub>gen</sub> = 0, ΔS = 0. Irreversible adiabatic (friction, stirring): ΔS > 0.
Entropy of an adiabatic closed system can never decrease.
Exam tip: 'Adiabatic' ≠ 'isentropic' unless the process is also reversible.

questions.text: A reversible heat engine takes heat from a source at 900 K and rejects heat to the atmosphere at 300 K. All its work drives a reversible heat pump that takes heat from the atmosphere at 300 K and delivers it to a building at 350 K, as shown. The heat delivered to the building per kJ of heat taken from the 900 K source (round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Chain the two devices through their common work: W = ηHEQ1 and Qbuilding = COPHP × W.
Qbuilding/Q1 = 0.6667 × 7 = 4.67
Exam tip: More heat reaches the building than leaves the source: the heat pump pulls extra energy from the atmosphere.

questions.text: 1 kg of ice at 0 °C melts completely to water at 0 °C (latent heat 333.5 kJ/kg). The entropy change of the ice (in kJ/K, round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Melting at constant temperature is internally reversible: ΔS = Q/T with T in kelvin.
Exam tip: Using 0 °C instead of 273.15 K is the classic mistake (it would divide by zero).

questions.text: A particular integral of y″ − 4y′ + 4y = e<sup>2x</sup> is
solution: Concept: The auxiliary equation (m − 2)² = 0 has a double root 2, which matches the exponent of the RHS; so try yp = A x² e2x.
For (D − 2)²y = e<sup>2x</sup>: y<sub>p</sub> = x²e<sup>2x</sup>/2! (rule for a root repeated twice)
Check: with y = (x²/2)e2x, (D − 2)y = x e2x and (D − 2)²y = e2x ✓, so yp = (x²/2) e2x
Exam tip: If eax on the RHS repeats a root k times, multiply the trial solution by xk.

questions.text: The solution of dy/dx = −2xy with y(0) = 3 is evaluated at x = 1. The value of y(1) (round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Variables separable: dy/y = −2x dx.
ln y = −x² + C ⇒ y = 3e<sup>−x²</sup> using y(0) = 3
Exam tip: Always apply the initial condition before substituting the final x.

questions.text: If F(s) is the Laplace transform of f(t) = e<sup>−2t</sup> cos 3t, the value of F(1) is
solution: Concept: First shifting theorem: L{e−atg(t)} = G(s + a), with L{cos bt} = s/(s² + b²).
Exam tip: Shift s, not t: replacing s by s − 2 instead of s + 2 gives (−1)/(1 + 9) = −1/10, a common slip.

questions.text: A room is kept at 22 °C by an electric resistance heater when the outdoor temperature is 2 °C. Treating the outdoors as the dead state, the second-law efficiency of the heater (in %, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: ηII = minimum work needed / actual work used. The minimum is a reversible heat pump between 275.15 K and 295.15 K.
COP<sub>rev</sub> = 295.15/20 = 14.76; the heater has COP = 1
Exam tip: First-law efficiency of a resistance heater is 100 %, yet it wastes over 93 % of the exergy of electricity.

questions.text: For an incompressible liquid, the difference between the specific heats c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> is
opts: T v β²/κ, which is large
solution: Concept: General relation: cp − cv = T v β²/κ (β = volume expansivity, κ = isothermal compressibility).
For an incompressible substance v is constant, so β = 0 and c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = 0.
So liquids and solids have a single specific heat c.
Exam tip: cp ≥ cv always, because κ > 0 for every stable substance.

questions.text: In a process the total entropy generated is 0.4 kJ/K. The surroundings are at 27 °C. The lost work (irreversibility) is
solution: Concept: Gouy–Stodola theorem: I = T₀Sgen, with T₀ in kelvin.
Exam tip: Using 27 instead of 300.15 gives 10.8 kJ, the trap option.

questions.text: A furnace wall has 0.2 m of firebrick (k = 1.2 W/m·K) on the inside and 0.1 m of insulating brick (k = 0.15 W/m·K) outside it. The inner face is at 900 °C and the outer face at 60 °C. The temperature at the firebrick–insulation interface (in °C) is ______
solution: Concept: Same heat flux through both layers; find q from the total resistance, then step through the first layer.
Exam tip: Check from the other side: 60 + 1008 × 0.6667 = 732 °C ✓.

questions.text: A bare steam pipe has an outer radius larger than the critical radius of insulation. Adding insulation to it will
opts: first increase and then decrease the heat loss
solution: Concept: Heat loss versus outer radius peaks at rc = k/h.
If the bare radius already exceeds r<sub>c</sub>, we are on the falling side of the curve: every extra layer reduces heat loss.
This is the normal case for steam pipes (r<sub>c</sub> of a few mm to a few cm).
Exam tip: The 'increase first' behaviour matters only for thin wires and small tubes.

questions.text: A spherical liquid-nitrogen vessel has an inner radius of 0.5 m and is covered with 50 mm of insulation (k = 0.02 W/m·K). The inner surface is at −196 °C and the outer surface at 25 °C. The heat gain (in W, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Spherical shell: Q = 4πk r₁r₂(T₂ − T₁)/(r₂ − r₁).
Exam tip: At this heat gain about 305.5/199 000 ≈ 1.5 g of N₂ boils off per second (hfg ≈ 199 kJ/kg).
